title: The Righteousness of King Anushirwan
summary: King Anushirwan the Just, while riding with his wise vizier Buzurjmihr through a desolate border province of Persia, halted their steeds near the ruins of an ancient, abandoned ...
full_text:
King Anushirwan the Just, while riding with his wise vizier Buzurjmihr through a desolate border province of Persia, halted their steeds near the ruins of an ancient, abandoned village. The stone cottages were crumbling, the irrigation canals were choked with weeds, and the fruit trees had withered into thorns.

Upon the broken wall of an ancient watchtower sat two large horned owls, hooting mournfully to each other in the dusk.

Anushirwan turned to his vizier, who was renowned for his knowledge of ancient sciences, and asked: 'Can you interpret for me what these two owls are speaking to each other with such sorrowful cries?'

Buzurjmihr lowered his head and answered with tactful gravity: 'Sire, the two owls are arranging a marriage between their children. The male owl says: "I will give my daughter to your son on condition that you grant her fifty ruined villages as her dowry!" And the second owl replies: "If King Anushirwan’s governors continue their current oppression and unjust taxation for another two years, I shall easily grant you a thousand ruined villages!"'

The words struck Anushirwan like a bolt of lightning! He realized with agonizing clarity that while he sat in his gilded palace in Ctesiphon listening to flattering courtiers, his corrupt governors were bleeding the countryside dry, driving the peasants from their homes and leaving the land a wilderness for owls.

The king wept in profound repentance. He returned immediately to his capital, dismissed the corrupt governors, canceled unjust taxes, and established a public court of appeal where any peasant could sound a golden bell in the palace square to demand royal justice.

Within five years, the villages were rebuilt, the canals flowed with fresh water, and the desert bloomed into gardens, immortalizing Anushirwan as the paragon of righteous kings.
moral: A ruler must listen to the silent ruined stones of his realm, for injustice destroys the foundation of empires.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
